posts.title: How we make money (and why it matters to you)
posts.body:
Every analytics tool makes money somehow. If you can't tell how, it's worth asking.

Here's how Plausible makes money: site owners pay us a subscription. That's the whole model.

We're independent. We're self-funded. We're profitable. We're based in the EU. And we don't sell customer data.

That last point isn't a line in a policy we could quietly rewrite later. It's how the business works. Our revenue comes from over 21,000 paying subscribers, not from what their visitors do.

Why this should matter to you:
→ When a tool is free, it's fair to ask what pays for it.
→ When you pay, you're the customer. Our incentives line up with yours.
→ There's no outside investor waiting for us to find a new revenue stream in your data.

Plausible isn't free, and it isn't the right fit for every analytics use case. We'd rather say that up front.

But if you want clear website stats and a straight answer about where the data goes, it's worth a look.

posts.title: Is your cookie banner there because of your analytics?
posts.body:
A lot of cookie banners exist because of one script: analytics.

Plausible doesn't use cookies and doesn't collect personal data. So you don't need a cookie banner or a GDPR consent form for it.

That means your visitors land on your page, not on a pop-up. And you count every visit, not only the people who clicked "accept".

One honest caveat: analytics is rarely the only script on a site. Ad pixels, chat widgets and embeds can have their own rules. Check your whole stack, and ask your own counsel if you're unsure.

posts.title: Your analytics script shouldn't slow the site it measures
posts.body:
It's odd when the tool measuring your site speed makes your site slower.

That's one reason we kept Plausible's script small. It's 54 times smaller than Google Analytics.

Why that matters:
→ Less code for every visitor to download.
→ Helps keep your pages fast, especially on mobile.
→ One less thing to fight when you're working on site speed.

You still get the numbers most site owners actually check: where visitors come from and what they read. On one page.

If you're a publisher, a store or a SaaS team watching page speed, it's worth seeing how much your current analytics adds.

posts.title: Analytics script size
posts.body:
Google Analytics' script is 54 times the size of the one we ship at Plausible.

Say you've run a speed test on your pricing page and seen third-party scripts flagged. Analytics is usually one of them. The browser has to download it, parse it and run it, and your visitor waits through that along with everything else on the page.

[NEEDS FACT: what are the actual file sizes of the two scripts, which tool did you measure them with, and on what date? The 54x should sit next to real numbers.]

A smaller script leaves less to fetch, which helps keep the page fast. I won't put a load-time gain on it, because that depends on the rest of your page.

[NEEDS FACT: what did you decide not to build to keep the script this small, and who asked for it?]

Here's a ten-minute audit. Open your browser's network tab, sort by size and find your analytics script. Then ask whether the report it feeds is one you opened this month. If not, you're making every visitor download something you don't use.

What would you give up in your analytics tool to make your key pages load faster, and what would you refuse to lose?

posts.title: The cookie banner that stays
posts.body:
You switched analytics tools and the cookie banner is still there.

If that's you, the banner may no longer be about analytics. Something else on the page could be setting cookies: an ad pixel, a chat widget, an embedded video.

[NEEDS FACT: describe one real support question where a customer still had a banner after switching. What turned out to be setting the cookies? Anonymise the customer.]

So make a list. Write down every third-party script on your site, then open your browser's developer tools and check which ones set cookies. If analytics was the only one, you may have a reason to rethink the banner. If it wasn't, you now know which tool is the reason, and you can decide whether it's worth keeping.

Whether you can drop the banner is a legal call for you and your adviser. I can only tell you what our product does: Plausible uses no cookies and collects no personal data, so it needs no cookie banner or GDPR consent form of its own.

Plausible isn't right for every analytics use case, and our About page says so.

Say you've opened Google Analytics to find one number and couldn't. We built for that person: a site owner who wants clear numbers on one page, without training. If your team builds deep custom reports every week, a bigger tool may fit you better.

I'd rather you hear that before you pay us. What I can show instead is how we're run: independent, self-funded, profitable, based in the EU, and we don't sell customer data. Over 21,000 paying subscribers fund the work, and we've tracked over 313 billion pageviews.

[NEEDS FACT: what words did a customer use, verbatim, about leaving Google Analytics? Do you have permission to quote them?]

Before you pick or switch any tool, write down the questions you ask your numbers every week. If one page answers them, a long report menu is just more to maintain. If it doesn't, choose the tool that does, even if it isn't ours.

I think most small sites outgrow custom reports less often than they fear. Where did you hit the wall with a simple analytics tool, if you did?

posts.title: No cookies in analytics means one less reason for a cookie banner
posts.body:
A cookie banner on every page of your site, just so your analytics can count visits. That's a lot of friction for a page-view number.

Plausible doesn't use cookies and doesn't collect personal data. Nothing personal is stored on the visitor's device and nothing personal is collected, so there's no GDPR consent form to show for analytics.

That changes two things for a site owner. Visitors land on your page instead of a pop-up. And people who would have clicked "reject" still get counted, because there's nothing for them to reject.

One honest limit. If your site also loads ad pixels, chat widgets or embedded videos that set cookies, those still need consent. Cookie-free analytics takes one item off the banner. Whether the banner goes away depends on everything else you load.

So before you change any tool, open your site in a private window and check which cookies are set before anyone clicks anything. Write down what each one is for. If analytics is the only reason your banner exists, that's the first thing to change.

For anyone who has removed their cookie banner: which script was the hardest one to give up?

posts.title: The analytics script is the one script every visitor loads
posts.body:
Your analytics script loads on every page, for every visitor, on every connection. Plausible's is 54 times smaller than Google Analytics.

That matters because analytics is the one script you never skip. A large hero image only loads on the homepage. The tracking script runs everywhere, including on the phone of someone on a train with one bar of signal.

We kept ours small by keeping it to its job: counting visits without cookies and without collecting personal data. Less code to download means less for the browser to fetch and run before your page is done.

You can check what your current setup costs in a couple of minutes. Open your site in Chrome, open DevTools, go to the Network tab and reload the page. Filter by your analytics provider's domain and look at the transfer size of every request it makes, then compare that with the size of your logo.

If your analytics outweighs your logo, you've found a speed fix that needs no redesign and no new hosting.

What's the heaviest script on your site that nobody on the team remembers adding?

Every analytics tool on your site answers to whoever pays for it. Before you install one, ask who that is and what the tool does with your visitors.

posts.title: Who pays for your analytics?
posts.body:
"Free" analytics is usually paid for with something. Worth asking what.

Here's how Plausible works:

• Independent and self-funded. No investors pushing for growth at any cost.
• Profitable, so the business runs on what customers pay.
• Based in the EU.
• We don't sell customer data.

More than 21,000 paying subscribers have chosen that model, and Plausible has tracked over 313 billion pageviews.

It isn't the right tool for every analytics need, and we'd rather say so up front. But if you want clear numbers from a company whose only customer is you, take a look. Link in the comments.
